topic.title: Every money trap the middle class falls into, explained

title: Every money trap the middle class falls into, explained
description:
Why does a raise never seem to change your bank balance?
Rohan earns more every year and still runs in place. This video follows him through six money traps that never feel like mistakes: the life that grows with every raise, the new car, the safe cash, the small charges that never stop, the bigger house and the one that costs the most of all.
Count how many you are in.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:24 The life that grows
1:27 The new car
2:18 The safe cash
3:10 The small charges
4:35 The bigger house
5:31 I'll start later

An animated story with illustrative numbers; the characters are not advisers.
Speak to a licensed financial adviser in your country before making financial decisions.
Illustrative only. Not financial advice.

lines.text: Rohan just got a raise. His treadmill got faster, but his bank balance didn't move. Why? Six money traps take the raise before he sees it. Here's how.
Here they are: the life that grows, the new car, the safe cash, the small charges, the bigger house, and the worst one, saved for last.
Six traps? How many of them am I in right now?
Count them as we go. Most families I knew were caught in more than one, and none of them noticed.
Each trap feels like a reward or a smart choice, which is exactly why it works, and why the treadmill keeps speeding up.
Trap one. The life that grows.
Trap one starts the day the raise lands: a nicer place, more takeout, and every bit of it feels earned.
Say his whole life costs $3,000 a month today: the rent, the food, the phone and the fun.
That sounds normal. So how is spending my own raise a trap?
Because prices climb: at an assumed 3% a year, that same life costs $5,418 a month in 20 years.
His pay goes up with each raise, but his spending climbs by the same amount, so the gap between the two never grows.
Every year the rent, the groceries and the phone plan creep up, until the same life costs $2,418 more each month.
And each new raise buys a bigger version of the same life, so the treadmill speeds up just to keep him in place.
By then that's $29,020 more every year, just to live exactly the way he lives today.
That's called lifestyle creep: each raise first covers rising prices, and spending the rest on a bigger life keeps the savings flat.
Over those 20 years, the rising price of that same life adds up to $276,353 more than today's price.
I watched it happen for my whole career. The raise was spent before the first new payslip ever arrived.
Then a different trap pulls into the driveway, shiny and new. So why does it still cost him money years after it stops being new?
Trap two. The new car.
My old car still runs fine. But I earned a new one, right?
So he signs for a $45,000 car, on a loan at an assumed 8% a year, for 6 years.
That's $789 every month, and $11,808 of it goes to interest, money that buys no car at all.
Rohan pays $56,808 in total over the loan, for a car with a sticker price of $45,000.
Meanwhile the car loses value every year. At an assumed steady drop, after 6 years it's worth $16,972.
Hold on. So I paid all that interest, and I'm left holding a car worth a fraction of the price?
And the trap is the loop: the loan ends, the car looks old, he signs for a new one, and the payments start again.
The car itself isn't the trap. Replacing it every few years, on a fresh loan each time, is what keeps him running.
A car is a depreciating asset: it loses value every year, and a loan adds interest on top of the loss.
Two traps, and both of them felt like rewards. So which trap would ever feel like being careful?
Trap three. The safe cash.
Rohan is careful with his savings. He keeps $20,000 in a big-bank savings account paying an assumed 0.4% a year.
Cash in a bank can't lose. What could possibly go wrong with that?
His bank pays him 0.4% a year, while prices climb at 3%, so his cash falls a little further behind each year.
Many big-bank savings accounts pay this little, because the bank lends that same money out to borrowers at much higher rates.
At 0.4% a year, in 10 years his cash grows to only $20,815.
Measured in today's money, that pile only buys what $15,488 buys now.
So my safe money is actually shrinking while it sits there? How did I never notice?
Because the jar looks fuller every year, while the things it can buy melt away underneath it.
That's $4,512 of buying power gone in 10 years, from money that never left the bank.
Cash is safe from a crash, yes. It just isn't safe from prices, and prices never take a year off.
At least Rohan can see that loss if he does the sum. So what about the charges so small he never even looks?
Trap four. The small charges that never stop.
Streaming, music, cloud storage, and a gym he rarely visits: each one takes a little every month.
They're tiny, though. What's the harm in a few little apps?
Together they come to $120 a month, which is $1,440 every single year.
And because every charge renews by itself, he never decides to keep paying. The payments simply carry on.
The gym takes its fee every month, whether he goes or not, and he hasn't been since the spring.
Then there's the app he tried free for a week and forgot. The trial ended long ago, but the charge never did.
Over 10 years, those little charges add up to $14,400, for things he barely uses.
Rohan tries one question on each app: would he sign up again today? For half of them, the answer is no.
Subscriptions at least show up on a statement. But what about a charge that never shows up anywhere at all?
Rohan finally invests. His $100,000 sits in a fund that charges an assumed 1% a year.
Such a tiny percentage? Why would I ever worry about that?
On $100,000, that's $1,000 a year, and the fee is taken whether the fund does well or badly.
Even if the pot never grew, 30 years of it is $30,000 in fees, before counting the growth that money never got to earn.
The fee drips out of the fund every year, and every coin that leaves it stops growing for good.
And the fee grows as the fund grows, because it's a share of the whole pot, not a flat charge.
Fund fees differ a lot, so the very same pot keeps far more of its own growth just by paying less for it.
The fee nobody reads is still a fee everybody pays, every year, in good markets and bad ones.
The name for it is the expense ratio, printed in the small print that so few people ever open.
That's four traps you can spot once someone points at them. So what makes the last two so much harder to see?
Trap five. The bigger house.
But a house is an investment, isn't it? So a bigger house must be better.
A $300,000 mortgage over 360 monthly payments, at an assumed 6.5%, costs $1,896 a month.
Stretch to a $400,000 house, and the payment jumps to $2,528, which is $632 more every month.
Across the whole loan, the bigger house costs $127,544 more in interest alone, before the bigger bills for heat and repairs.
So what does the bigger house cost me in total, once every payment is made?
He pays $910,178 for the bigger house in the end, against $682,633 for the home he actually needs.
The extra room is never the expensive part. The extra payment is, every month of the loan, and every one comes with a bill.
A house he can afford leaves room for every other goal. A house that stretches him leaves room for none.
From the street, Rohan's bigger house looks like success.
Five traps so far, and each one costs money he can see. The last one costs nothing at all today. So why is it the worst?
Trap six. I'll start later.
I'll start investing when I earn more. What's the rush, really?
And this is the twist. Starting late, Rohan saves only $36,000 less in total. But at the end, he's $299,029 behind.
Here's how. Plan A starts today. Plan B starts later. And both of them stop on exactly the same day, the day Rohan retires.
Plan A puts $300 a month into investments for 35 years, growing at an assumed 7% a year.
When he retires, all those small monthly amounts have grown into $543,468, far more than he ever put in.
Plan B waits, then puts in the same amount for only 25 years. That grows to $244,439, less than half as much.
Plan B puts in $90,000 of his own money, and Plan A puts in $126,000: more, but not that much more on paper.
Hold on. I save almost the same money and still end up that far behind? How?
That's because early money has years to earn on its own earnings, and those last years are where the tree grows biggest.
This is compounding, and the one thing it needs most is the one thing waiting takes away: time.
No bill ever arrives for waiting, yet it's the biggest cost on the list: $299,029, just for starting later.
Every young man I lent money to thought time was the one thing he had plenty of. None of them was right.
Six traps: the creep, the car, the cash, the small charges, the house and later. Each one took a slice of every raise.
So that's why the raise never moved his balance: six traps took their share first. One rule for each, and Rohan finally steps off the treadmill.
Rohan's way out: he spends less than each raise, reads the fees, and starts early. So which trap are you in right now? Tell me the number.
Illustrative numbers with assumed rates. Which trap are you in? Comment the number below.

c1-term/c1-total: trap one labels pure inflation as lifestyle creep. c1-prices..c1-total compute what the SAME life costs at an assumed 3% (price_rise), then c1-term calls it lifestyle creep and the c1-total card 'What creep costs' plus the HUD 'Cost of the traps' counts $276,353 as the trap's cost. That cost is inflation, which happens whether or not Rohan spends his raise, so the number does not support the conclusion. Fix: retitle the c1-total card (e.g. 'Same life, 20 years on'), keep it out of the 'Cost of the traps' counter, and say the creep is what comes on top: each raise first has to cover rising prices, and spending the rest is what leaves savings flat.

c3-grows: 'With assumed inflation of 3%, in 10 years his cash grows to only $20,815' is wrong: the cash grows to $20,815 because of the 0.4% interest (the on-screen equation is $20,000 + 0.4% a year), not because of inflation. Fix: 'At 0.4% a year, in 10 years his cash grows to only $20,815.' and move the equation trigger from 'inflation' to a word in the new line.

c3-why: 'Easy-access savings pay little' is not true in general: US high-yield easy-access savings accounts pay a few percent (channel profile: US savings 3-5%). Only the typical big-bank account pays around 0.4%. Fix: 'Many big-bank savings accounts pay this little, because the bank lends that same money out at much higher rates.' and in c3-jar say 'a big-bank savings account'.

c5-year/c5-total: 'that fee is $1,000 every single year, whether the fund does well or badly' (header 'Every year, no matter what') and 'at least $30,000 in fees' are wrong for a percentage fee: 1% of a pot that falls is less than $1,000, and c5-share itself says the fee moves with the pot. Fix c5-year: 'On $100,000, that's $1,000 a year, and the fee is taken whether the fund does well or badly.' (header 'Taken every year'); c5-total: 'Even if the pot never grew, 30 years of it is $30,000 in fees, before counting the growth that money never got to earn.'

c6-sharma: 'The extra years of payments are [the expensive part]' (word overlay 'Years') is false: both mortgages are 360 months (small_months = big_months = 360); the bigger house costs a bigger payment, not more years. Fix: 'The extra payment is, every month for thirty years, and every one comes with a bill.' and change the word overlay to 'Every month'.

recap: 'Spend less than each raise, read the fees, and start early.' tells the viewer what to do with their money in the imperative (rule 4), and the recap equation shows 'Spend less + read fees = Start early'. Fix: 'Rohan's way out: he spends less than each raise, reads the fees, and starts early. So which trap are you in right now? Tell me the number.' Also reframe the payoff rules card (all imperatives: 'Save half of a raise', 'Keep the car longer', 'Beat rising prices', 'Check every fee', 'Buy what you need', 'Start now') as what Rohan does, e.g. 'He saves half of each raise', 'He keeps the car longer', 'He starts now'.
